interview_context.setting_or_workflow_context: Group discussion about AI-generated oncology literature-review reports for clinical information seeking, note support, and treatment-decision support.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I can see it becoming useful, it's just, I'm, like, very particular when I want to look up information, and so none of the reports, I guess, like, satisfied everything that I look for, in, like, one report.
segments.rationale: The participant explicitly says the reports could become useful, but also says none satisfied everything they look for. This supports both future potential and unmet format/content needs.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: Like, I think the yellow reports just have it, a list of 30 different references, and everything was just, like, conjected together, and it wasn't… Yeah, I agree with that. I think visually, how it's laid out makes a big difference.
segments.rationale: The participant criticizes a long, crowded reference list and directly links layout to usability. The excerpt grounds codes about overload and visual parsing difficulty.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I like the sections. So, I like the fact that it had a section on efficacy, and one regimen to the other, and report, and then another on toxicity. So, like, yeah, definitely putting things into different sections is helpful.
segments.rationale: The participant positively evaluates reports that separate content into named sections and highlights efficacy, regimen comparison, and toxicity as useful categories.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: The actual data as in their, like, they had overall survival, everybody's survival. Yeah, especially, like, when it just gets to blocks of text, like, the paragraphs get too long, then, like, I immediately am less interested.
segments.rationale: The participant values concrete outcome data while also saying long paragraphs reduce engagement. This supports both a positive preference and a negative reaction.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I think pink was my second favorite, because I thought, like, the chart format was interesting. And it would be helpful in specific clinical instances... but then for other questions, it would probably be unnecessary.
segments.rationale: The participant says the format is useful in some clinical scenarios but unnecessary in others, indicating context-dependent rather than universal value.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: Probably both. Yeah. Yeah, I mean, like, a customizable format would be nice, because there are ways I like it tailored, but if there were pre-formats that we can sort of, like, build off of at some level.
segments.rationale: The participant wants both tailored outputs and starting templates, indicating a preference for flexible customization without requiring everything from scratch.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: The very thorough, in-depth, red or blue, I think, is very helpful. I particularly like the blue if I needed something to kind of help frame a note... The pink one had the table? But I don't think standalone that's good.
segments.object_of_evaluation: depth, note-writing support, and table usefulness
segments.rationale: The participant values detailed reports for unfamiliar scenarios and note framing, but says tables alone are insufficient. This supports a mixed view tied to context.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: In terms of actually making a decision for a patient, that's not the format that I would want. And the formatting of the tables in pink and a little in yellow, there were times where it was hard to know where, like, one cell started, and the next one ended.
segments.rationale: The participant directly rejects this table-heavy format for patient decision-making and describes cell boundaries as visually unclear, increasing cognitive effort.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: Like, if it's, like, a key figure that's really highlighting, like, either supporting or not supporting whatever clinical decision you're trying to make, then it's helpful... I like hard, deterministic data, from the primary source.
segments.object_of_evaluation: figures, evidence provenance, and source access
segments.rationale: The participant values figures when they directly support a decision and explicitly prefers concrete primary-source data, grounding trust in source material.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: We have, like, a hyperlink, too. Like, if you have that where you just click on, and it takes you to that exact reference, and, like, that Graph within reference, that would be helpful.
segments.rationale: The participant wants links to the exact reference and even the relevant graph, indicating a desire for faster source verification and precise navigation.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: Some of them were good because they basically just, like, summarized, you know, like, NCCN guidelines or, like, other already established bodies... I would prefer to just, like, have the information presented neutrally.
segments.rationale: The participant likes summaries of established guidance but prefers neutral presentation over model-generated recommendations, showing a preference boundary.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I didn't feel comfortable making decisions just based off of what I was reading. I mean, they provided great evidence, but, I feel like it was just sort of, like, a little bit ambiguous for some parts.
segments.rationale: The participant acknowledges evidence quality but says ambiguity prevented comfortable decision-making, indicating that evidence alone did not create actionability.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I like when it says, here are all the arguments for, and here are all the arguments against, and then it kind of synthesizes everything together... as long as they can actually put the arguments where they need to be.
segments.rationale: The participant values structured pros/cons synthesis, but only when arguments are correctly organized. This indicates appreciation with an accuracy condition.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I just think there's still so many instances where the data isn't fully accurate, and doctors don't have a lot of trust... I'm gonna go through all of the things that they're citing anyway to make sure that they're accurately saying what was in the reports.
segments.rationale: The participant links incomplete accuracy to low trust and explains that they still verify cited material themselves, reducing the system's time-saving value.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: Kind of like the way that it reads in a paper... they'll put a superscript with a link to the reference for that, so I find, like, that's just how I read naturally... if you hover over it, and then you see, like, a little snapshot.
segments.rationale: The participant prefers literature-like inline citation patterns and proposes hover previews, showing how familiar scholarly reading conventions support usability.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I think the blue report did a great job of providing, like, the reference if you could copy and paste it into a search engine to find it... but [the other report] wouldn't provide, like, the links or the clear-cut data that you can kind of quickly search it.
segments.rationale: The participant compares reports based on how easy it is to identify and search cited sources, praising one and criticizing another for weaker linkage to evidence.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I think this is useful to have. I actually think that sometimes it saves me time, in terms of if I have a specific question, and I'm looking for evidence on open evidence, then it gives me the exact citations to review.
segments.rationale: The participant explicitly states the tool can save time for specific questions because it surfaces exact citations to review.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: It's also useful to go through the logic of a particular patient scenario... So overall, I think it has the potential to save time, especially in a busy clinic kind of scenario.
segments.object_of_evaluation: clinical reasoning support and workflow speed
segments.rationale: The participant describes the system as useful for reasoning through scenarios and specifically ties value to time pressure in clinic.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: It would also be good to, to have... like, a short summary of why it's providing that source. You know, like, this was the trial, and this was, like, these were the primary outcomes. And then the link.
segments.rationale: The participant does not want bare links; they want a concise summary explaining why the citation matters, including trial identity and primary outcomes.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: If there are a way to make this, like, PHI, like, fully integrated and remember me? Because I think my ChatGPT is nice, because it knows me, so it knows what I want out of it, memory format already.
segments.rationale: The participant asks for a system that can be integrated into clinical constraints while remembering their preferred format, indicating desire for personalized and usable deployment.

themes.theme_name: Usability depends on readable structure, not just having more information
themes.theme_definition: Participants repeatedly tied usefulness to how information was organized and displayed. They favored sectioned reports with concrete outcomes and disliked dense paragraphs, crowded references, and visually confusing tables. Across comments, readability shaped whether the same evidence felt actionable or burdensome.

representative_quotes.quote: I like the sections... definitely putting things into different sections is helpful.
When it just gets to blocks of text... I immediately am less interested.

themes.confidence_basis: Repeated across multiple participants and multiple parts of the transcript.

themes.theme_name: Clinicians want evidence retrieval and source traceability more than unsupported recommendation-making
themes.theme_definition: Participants valued reports that linked clearly to underlying literature, especially when exact references, figures, or source passages were easy to access. At the same time, they were uneasy relying on outputs for decisions when recommendations felt ambiguous or insufficiently separated from source evidence. Trust was strongest when the report behaved like an expedited literature search rather than an autonomous decider.

representative_quotes.quote: I like hard, deterministic data, from the primary source.
I didn't feel comfortable making decisions just based off of what I was reading.

themes.confidence_basis: Strong support from repeated comments about citations, links, neutral presentation, ambiguity, and verification.

themes.theme_name: The right output should be customizable to the task, the user, and the level of familiarity
themes.theme_definition: Participants did not describe one universally best format. Instead, they wanted different output types for deep dives, quick refreshers, note support, and specific decision contexts. They also wanted a mix of presets and customization, ideally with remembered personal preferences.

representative_quotes.quote: A customizable format would be nice... but if there were pre-formats that we can sort of, like, build off of.
My ChatGPT is nice, because it knows me, so it knows what I want out of it.

themes.confidence_basis: Multiple participants raised tailoring, preset formats, scenario-specific outputs, and remembered preferences.

analytic_memos.summary: Participants generally saw promise in AI-generated literature-review reports, but they did not describe any single current format as sufficient. The strongest positive reactions centered on readable structure, exact citations, concrete data, and outputs that behave like an efficient literature search rather than a black-box recommender. Participants wanted reports to be easier to scan, with sections, concise summaries, and better citation UX. They were notably less comfortable when the output blurred neutral evidence presentation with model-generated recommendation. Trust remained limited because some participants still felt compelled to verify every cited source manually. The preferred future state was not one fixed report, but a set of customizable or templated modes matched to different tasks such as note-writing, quick refreshers, or deep dives. Personalization and privacy-compatible integration were also raised as meaningful product opportunities.
tensions_or_tradeoffs: More detail can be helpful for unfamiliar topics, but too much text becomes hard to read.
Tables and charts can speed review, but standalone structured outputs may be insufficient for actual patient decisions.
Participants want summaries to save time, but not at the cost of source traceability and verification.
Some synthesis is helpful, but users still want clear separation between neutral evidence and any recommendation.
